problem: Zero-shot LLM-based goal-oriented navigation methods are built for one goal type: ESC and SG-Nav handle object categories, Mod-IIN handles instance images, and InstructNav covers only language goals. Universal methods such as GOAT and PSL need expensive RL training and overfit to simulation. No training-free framework handles object-category, instance-image and text-description goals with one model.
motivation: Real instructions come in many forms, so a single agent should accept any goal type without retraining. Encoding scene and goal as text loses structure. The authors observe that the scene, a category, an image and a description can all be expressed as the same kind of object-relation graph. With a shared format, goal search becomes explicit graph matching and alignment that an LLM can reason over.
key_idea: Represent every goal and the online scene as graphs of the same form, compute a graph-matching score between them, and use that score to switch between three LLM-driven exploration strategies (zero, partial and perfect match), with a blacklist that prevents re-matching failed hypotheses.
insight: The matching score is useful because it decides when to change strategy, and the blacklist lets the agent recover from wrong matches. On HM3D-IIN, removing the blacklist drops SR from 60.2 to 50.6, the largest ablation drop, because the agent keeps re-matching failed nodes and gets stuck. Removing the score computation (switching stages on any match) gives 54.9, and replacing stage 1 with plain frontier-based exploration gives 55.1. The graph machinery pays off mainly when the goal has structure: IIN improves by +4.1 SR over Mod-IIN, while object-goal gains over SG-Nav are only +0.5 to +0.8 SR, since the goal graph is then a single node. In that case the authors attribute the gain to stage-3 scene-graph correction and goal verification (removing verification costs 2.0 SR on IIN).
method: Uniform goal graph: an object goal becomes a single node. An image goal uses Grounded-SAM to find objects and LLaVA to name pairwise spatial relations as edges. A text goal is parsed by the LLM into a JSON node/edge graph with a central object o.
Online scene graph: built incrementally from posed RGB-D following SG-Nav; nodes are objects stored with world coordinates, and edges are text-described spatial or semantic relations.

Graph matching: node embedding = CLIP text embedding concatenated with node degree; edge embedding = CLIP text embedding. The similarity matrix is thresholded at τ=0.9 and bipartite matching yields matched nodes M_N and edges M_E. Topology score S_T = 1 − normalized graph-edit distance between the matched subgraph and the goal graph structure. Overall score S = (S_N+S_E+S_T)/3.

Stage 1, zero matching (S<σ1=0.5): the LLM splits the goal graph into internally correlated subgraphs. Each subgraph is turned into text and used as an object goal for SG-Nav's chain-of-thought frontier scoring, and one frontier is chosen by averaging frontier scores and distance to the agent.

Stage 2, partial matching (σ1≤S<σ2=0.9 with at least one anchor pair): the goal graph is projected to BEV by DFS from o placed at (0,0), prompting the LLM for each node's coordinates from edge relations. A 2D similarity transform (scale, rotation, translation) is solved from each anchor pair, the remaining goal nodes are mapped into the scene frame, and the long-term goal is the center of their minimum enclosing circle.

Stage 3, perfect matching (S>σ2 and o matched): scene-graph correction runs GCN-style LLM message passing over nodes and edges within distance d of o, using adjacency and incidence matrices plus a LLaVA description of the new image. Goal verification uses confidence C_t = N_t + M_t + S_t − λD_t, where N_t is the corrected proportion, M_t the LightGlue keypoint-match proportion (IIN only), S_t the matching score and D_t the path length since entering stage 3. o is accepted if C_t exceeds C_thr.

Blacklist and local policy: failed stage-2 anchor pairs and failed stage-3 matches are blacklisted and excluded from matching, and are un-blacklisted if later corrected. Long-term goals are turned into move_forward/turn/stop actions by a Fast Marching Method local planner.

setting.backbone: LLaMA-2-7B (LLM, frozen) + LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B (VLM, frozen); also frozen CLIP text encoder, Grounded-SAM, LightGlue
setting.observation: egocentric posed RGB-D (RGB + depth + pose); goal given as category text, instance image, or text description
setting.action_space: LLM/geometry-predicted long-term goal points executed by an FMM local planner with discrete move_forward / turn_left / turn_right / stop
setting.privileged: none beyond agent pose (posed RGB-D input)

numbers_note: The paper never names the evaluation splits or episode counts. 'val' and full-split evaluation are assumed from the cited protocols (SG-Nav for ObjNav, Mod-IIN for IIN, PSL/InstanceNav for TextNav). Only SR and SPL are reported. The conclusion claims a real-robot deployment, but the provided text has no real-world results. Ablations (Tables 2–3) are on HM3D-IIN only and are not listed as separate variants here.
results: UniGoal is the first single training-free model covering ObjNav, IIN and TextNav. It reaches 41.0/16.4 (MP3D ObjNav), 54.5/25.1 (HM3D ObjNav), 48.0/24.2 (RoboTHOR ObjNav), 60.2/23.7 (HM3D IIN) and 20.2/11.4 (HM3D TextNav) SR/SPL. Against task-specific zero-shot methods it beats SG-Nav by +0.8 SR on MP3D ObjNav and Mod-IIN (56.1) by +4.1 SR on IIN. Against supervised universal methods it beats GOAT by +3.9/1.0 on HM3D ObjNav, +22.8/7.6 on IIN and +3.2/2.6 on TextNav (SR/SPL). It still trails supervised IEVE on IIN (70.2 SR), OVRL-v2 on HM3D ObjNav (64.7 SR), and VLFM in HM3D ObjNav SPL (30.3).
limitations: Gains on ObjectNav are marginal (+0.5 SR over SG-Nav on HM3D) because the goal graph collapses to one node. It remains well below supervised specialists (IEVE on IIN, OVRL-v2 on HM3D ObjNav), and absolute TextNav SR is low (20.2).
Many hand-tuned thresholds (τ, σ1, σ2, d, λ, C_thr) and many LLM/VLM calls per step. Runtime and cost are not reported, and ablations cover only HM3D-IIN.
Evaluation details are sparse: splits and episode counts are unstated, the ObjNav success radius of 1.6 m looks non-standard, and the real-world deployment is only asserted in the conclusion.
